The claim, that the text does not tell where the link goes and nothing around it does, names that defect, so the label is true_positive.

The claim also describes the text as not saying where the link goes, not as naming a destination the link does not reach. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on both points, so the label is uncertain.

ref: #splide-news-list > li:nth-of-type(7) > a > div > img

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the photo of a news carousel slide (a Splide clone of slide 2, not aria-hidden, same image and alt as the original): an aerial view of Palmas behind the headline 'Tocantins ocupa 3o lugar nacional...'. Its alt is word for word the slide's subtitle, which is also visible text inside the same link, so the link name reads the subtitle twice and nothing describes the photo; the article page uses the same sentence as the photo's caption. The live homepage has the same alt, so the capture does not differ. elementFails: the photo is generic illustration that adds nothing the story needs, and the link already carries its purpose in text, so I would log the redundant alt as a best-practice issue rather than a 1.1.1 failure. But competent auditors would reasonably disagree: one can treat the photo as informative (its alt does not describe it) or as decorative with a non-null alt (F39, H2). Hence uncertain.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the photo in li 7 of the news carousel: a Splide loop clone (class splide__slide--clone) of slide 2, with the same img and alt as the real slide. The crop shows an aerial view of Palmas. Its alt is word for word the slide's blurb ('Estado registra um dos menores diferenciais de remuneração...'), which is already inside the h1 of the same link, so a screen reader reads it twice and learns nothing about the picture. elementFails: I lean yes. If the photo is decorative, F38 expects alt="". If it is informative, the alt is not an equivalent of what it shows. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same img and alt on slide 2. Splide sets aria-hidden on off-screen clones once the carousel stops moving; the snapshot caught li 7 without it, but this happens on the live page too, and the real slide carries the same alt. Label: an objection holds. A redundant alt on a supplementary photo inside a link that already has text is widely treated as a best-practice issue rather than a 1.1.1 failure; axe's image-redundant-alt rule, for example, is tagged best-practice. Whether a news photo counts as decorative is a judgment call, so competent auditors would reasonably disagree: uncertain.

It meets 2.4.4. The model had the destination heading and the news context, and judged from a generic page title. A generic page title is a 2.4.2 question for the destination page, not a 2.4.4 failure of this link. elementFails: the link text names the category it opens, so its purpose can be determined from the text; passes. captureDiffers: the live home page and the destination match the capture. ref: #bloco-header > div > div > form > div > input
subject: Pesquisar
message: The placeholder "Pesquisar" has a contrast of 2.85:1 with the field (#999999 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field (input name=termo), whose only text label is its placeholder "Pesquisar" (accessible name comes from the placeholder; there is no visible label). claimTrue: the snapshot's pixel measurement gives #999999 on #ffffff, 2.85:1, at 14px weight 400, and my own sampling of the screenshot at the field finds the darkest glyph pixels at #999999 on white (2.85:1). elementFails: the live site's stylesheet sets .form-control::-webkit-input-placeholder / ::-moz-placeholder to #999 on the default white field, so users get the same 2.85:1 for normal-size text, below 4.5:1 (and below 3:1). Placeholder text is text and falls under none of 1.4.3's exceptions (it is not incidental, not a logo, and the field is not inactive); here it is also the only text naming the field. captureDiffers: the full-page screenshot draws the fixed header lower down the page, but the colours, font and live CSS match, so nothing differs that touches contrast. The claim names exactly this failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search field (input.form-control, placeholder "Pesquisar", no label, so the placeholder is also its only accessible name). The snapshot's pixel measurement gives #999999 on #ffffff, 2.85:1, at 14px weight 400. I sampled the screenshot and the darkest placeholder pixels are exactly #999999 on a white field. I looked for a reason it could pass and found none. Understanding 1.4.3 (WCAG 2.1) says the criterion applies to text in the page, including placeholder text. 14px normal is not large text. The field is enabled, so the inactive-component exemption does not apply. It is neither decoration nor a logo, and it carries the field's purpose. The live page has the same input markup, and its CSS sets .form-control::-webkit-input-placeholder / ::-moz-placeholder to #999 with no override, on Bootstrap's white form-control. So users get the same 2.85:1, below 4.5:1, and the claim names that failure.

ref: #main-content
subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is , Drupal's empty fragment-target anchor before the main content: no href, no tabindex, no text, no rendered size (bounds null). claimTrue: the snapshot's CDP accessibility node does report role link with no name (the snapshot's own role field says generic), so the sentence about what the browser exposes holds of the capture. elementFails: 4.1.2 covers user interface components, parts of the content perceived as a control for a function. This anchor is not one: it has no destination, no content, no box to click and is not in the keyboard tab order; the live HTML has no skip link pointing to it either. It is a named anchor, not a link, and no keyboard or pointer user can operate it; whatever leads Chrome to map it to the link role does not make it a control. The live page serves the same markup, so captureDiffers is no. The rule treated any node the browser maps to a link role as a widget needing a name, which is broader than the criterion, hence criterion_misapplied. (At most this is cleanup advice to remove the vestigial anchor, not a 4.1.2 failure.)

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is , Drupal's empty skip-link target. It has no href, no content, no tabindex, no recorded listeners and no rendered box (bounds null). The claim is true of the capture: Chrome's CDP tree gives it the role link with no name. The screen-reader announcement in the claim is an inference the snapshot cannot show. But 4.1.2 asks for names on user interface components. Under the HTML spec, an a element without href is only a placeholder for a link. HTML-AAM maps it to generic, as Rampa's own role field does. The ACT link-name rule applies only to the semantic role link, and nothing on the page uses this element as a control. The live HTML has the same element, and no skip link even points to it. Users perceive nothing they could operate, so it is not a component and does not fail 4.1.2. The rule took Chrome's heuristic role as proof of a component and applied the naming requirement outside the criterion's scope.

ref: #portal-searchbox-field
subject: Buscar no portal
message: The placeholder "Buscar no portal" has a contrast of 2.85:1 with the field (#999999 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input type="text" id="portal-searchbox-field" class="searchField" placeholder="Buscar no portal" title="Buscar no portal" name="searchword">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The search field's placeholder 'Buscar no portal' is the only visible label of the field (its <label> is display:none). In Edge on the live page, the ::placeholder color is rgb(153,153,153) at 12px on an rgb(255,255,255) field, which is 2.85:1, below the 4.5:1 that 1.4.3 requires for normal-size text. The screenshot shows the same light grey text on white. The claim is accurate and names the failure. Capture and live page match.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the search field's placeholder 'Buscar no portal', 12px, weight 400. claimTrue: Bootstrap 2's input::-webkit-input-placeholder{color:#999999} applies and the field is white, so it is 2.85:1 as stated, and Understanding 1.4.3 says placeholder text is covered. The concrete reason it could still be wrong is G174, a sufficient technique for 1.4.3. The header has an 'Alto contraste' link (#dcffe3 on #045b14, about 7.3:1) whose script adds .contraste to div.layout, which wraps the header. In that mode '.contraste input' sets the field to #262626 (and #000 on focus). No high-contrast rule reaches this field's ::placeholder (the yellow rule targets the input itself and the #fff rule only .form-control), so the placeholder stays #999999 and gets about 5.3:1 (7.4:1 on focus), which meets 4.5:1. elementFails: on that reading the element meets 1.4.3 through G174. captureDiffers: the live CSS and HTML match what Rampa measured. Auditors differ on whether a high-contrast toggle lets a default presentation at 2.85:1 conform, and whether the alternate presentation conforms across the page was not checked: uncertain.

message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input type="text" id="portal-searchbox-field" class="searchField" placeholder="Buscar no portal" title="Buscar no portal" name="searchword">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header search input has a <label for> 'Busca:' with class 'hide' (display:none), plus title and placeholder 'Buscar no portal'. The snapshot's Chromium tree gives it an empty name. I loaded the live page in Edge (Chromium 157) and read its accessibility tree: the name is "", taken from the hidden label (value ""), and title and placeholder are marked as superseded, so neither is used. In Chrome and Edge, then, the textbox has no accessible name, which fails 4.1.2. The claim says this. Firefox may expose the hidden label's text, and a tool that reads only the markup (label plus title) might pass it, but what Chromium users receive is a textbox with no name. Live page and capture match.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search field <input id=portal-searchbox-field title="Buscar no portal" placeholder="Buscar no portal">, with <label for=portal-searchbox-field class=hide>Busca: </label>; .hide is display:none in Bootstrap. claimTrue: the snapshot's CDP tree gives the textbox the name "" with a labelledby relation to the hidden label, and no description, so the sentence holds for the capture. elementFails: the reasons it could be wrong are concrete. The markup carries an associated label (H44 test passes), a title (H65) and a placeholder, and Rampa's own name computation got 'Busca:'. Chromium apparently stops at the display:none label and returns an empty name without falling back to the title. Firefox and other engines may name it, and screen readers may still read the placeholder, so 'announces only textbox' is not shown. I could not load the page in a browser with a screen reader to see what users actually get. captureDiffers: the live HTML and CSS (.hide display:none, the same input and label) match the capture. ref: #edit-markup > a
subject: https://portal.fgv.br/protecao-dados-pessoais
message: The link text "https://portal.fgv.br/protecao-dados-pessoais" is an address, not a purpose.

patch.ref: #edit-markup > a
patch.before: https://portal.fgv.br/protecao-dados-pessoais
patch.after: Proteção de Dados Pessoais

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The link's text is the address https://portal.fgv.br/protecao-dados-pessoais, so the claim's sentence holds. But the link sits in the sentence '...você poderá se descadastrar a qualquer momento diretamente nas mensagens recebidas ou por meio do Portal do Titular, no link https://...', in the snapshot and in the live HTML. That sentence is programmatically determined link context and gives the purpose: the FGV Portal do Titular, where you manage your personal data and unsubscribe. The address's path says the same. It passes 2.4.4. WCAG does not forbid an address as link text when the context gives the purpose, so the claim applied a stricter rule.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link text is the URL https://portal.fgv.br/protecao-dados-pessoais (claimTrue: it is an address). But it sits in the same sentence as '...você poderá se descadastrar ... por meio do Portal do Titular, no link', which is programmatically determined context, and the URL itself reads as FGV's personal-data protection portal. Its purpose (the data-subject portal where one can unsubscribe) can be determined, so 2.4.4 is met. The finding applies a rule WCAG does not have, that a URL cannot state a purpose. The live HTML has the same sentence (the title '(opens in a new window)' is added by script and does not matter).

patch.after: <input id="email" type="email" class="title-small w-full break-words border-none bg-transparent text-colors-text" name="email" value="" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the newsletter sign-up field in the sidebar box 'Saiba investir melhor', labelled 'Seu e-mail' by a <label for=email>. It is <input id=email type=email name=email> with no autocomplete attribute. claimTrue is yes: no autocomplete in the capture, and the snapshot records Chrome's form issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError on this field, so 'Chromium's own form check flags it' holds. elementFails is yes. The field collects the user's own email address, which is an Input Purpose ('email') under 1.3.5. type=email gives the data format but not that this is the user's own address. Without autocomplete="email" (H98), the purpose is not programmatically determined. captureDiffers is no: the live server HTML has the same input with no autocomplete, and the screenshot shows the field rendered as captured.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Newsletter sign-up field ("Saiba investir melhor"), <input id=email type=email name=email> labelled "Seu e-mail", with no autocomplete attribute. It collects the user's own email address, an Input Purpose listed in WCAG 2.1 section 7; type=email gives the format, not whose address it is, and the only sufficient technique (H98) is missing. claimTrue: the snapshot shows no autocomplete and Chromium's form issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError on this input, so both parts hold. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the identical input with no autocomplete. I looked for a reason it could pass (not user data, purpose set another way) and found none: true_positive.

skeptic.rationale: Image link in a related-articles card: <a> > <figure> > span > img with alt ("Tombo das ações de IA derruba Nasdaq em 5,28% e provoca onda de perdas em Wall Street"), no text, no aria-label, aria-labelledby or title; the headline is a separate adjacent link to the same href. claimTrue: the snapshot's CDP tree gives this link the name "" (Rampa's own 'name' field is raw <noscript> markup, a collector quirk, but the finding rests on the browser name). subject: previous slider
message: The icon of this button ("previous slider") has at most 1.32:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#e0e0e0 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <button id="previous-arrow-categoriesCarousel" type="button" class="prev-arrow Arrow_prevArrow__koDoT CategoriesCarousel_arrow__HK3SW slick-arrow slick-prev slick-disabled" aria-label="previous slider">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: 'previous slider' arrow button of the partner-brand carousel. Its class includes slick-disabled: the carousel is at its first slide, so react-slick removes the click handler. Its icon is #e0e0e0 from the CSS, against #ffffff (1.32:1), while the active 'next slider' arrow is #191927 (17.36:1). The screenshot also shows the left arrow lighter than the right. The measured facts in the claim are true of the snapshot. But the light grey is the inactive state, and 1.4.11 does not apply to inactive components (Understanding 1.4.11: visible but not currently operable, not required to meet contrast). So the element does not fail 1.4.11. That the button stays focusable with no disabled or aria-disabled state is a possible 4.1.2 issue, not a 1.4.11 one. The arrows are script-rendered, and at load users get the same first-slide state, so there is no capture difference. The rule ignored the inactive exemption.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The "previous slider" arrow of the partner-brands carousel. Its class includes slick-disabled because the carousel starts at the first slide. The measured #e0e0e0 on white (1.32:1) is the disabled style. The "next slider" arrow, which is active, measures #191927 at 17.36:1 in the same snapshot. The screenshot shows the left arrow faint and the right one dark. In react-slick, a disabled arrow at slide 0 of a non-infinite carousel gets no click handler, so the control is visible but not currently operable. 1.4.11 exempts inactive components, and its Understanding document says they "are not required to meet contrast requirements". So the icon does not fail 1.4.11 in this state. Once the user advances, it turns dark. Not exposing the disabled state programmatically (no disabled or aria-disabled) would be a 4.1.2 matter, not a contrast failure. Users get the same initial state.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: [visual context] The link's accessible name and title are both 'Whatsapp'. Its href opens WhatsApp with this article's title and URL filled in, so its purpose is to share the article. The only thing that says 'share' is the bold 'Compartilhe' above the icons. That is a sibling div (heateor_sss_sharing_title), not a heading and not a list item or paragraph containing the link, so it does not count. The nearest preceding heading is the article's h1, which says nothing about sharing. 'Whatsapp' alone does not tell sharing apart from going to ABRALE on WhatsApp: the same bar's 'Instagram' link goes to ABRALE's Instagram profile, and the top bar's links named after networks are profile links. The purpose cannot be determined from the link text and its programmatic context, so it fails 2.4.4 and Rampa missed it. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same share bar markup.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: [visual context] This icon-only share link is named 'Whatsapp' (by aria-label and title) and leads to api.whatsapp.com/send with the article's title and URL. ref: #block-museucatavento-main-menu > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
subject: exposições
message: The text "exposições" has at most 2.64:1 contrast with what is behind it (#999999 on #f6f6f6), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a background image). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: Main-menu link 'exposições'. Snapshot and live stylesheet agree: '.menu li a' is #999999, bold, font-size clamp(11px,0.9vw,13px) = 11.5px at 1280 px, over the page's #f6f6f6 background: 2.64:1, under 4.5:1, and 11.5px bold is not large text. The claim's colours, size, ratio and the bgImage reason match the snapshot's pixelContrast record (claimTrue yes). Rampa hid the load popup overlay to measure; the live HTML and CSS are the same, so the capture matches what users see once the popup is closed (captureDiffers no). The page users receive also has a high-contrast toggle: the button 'Ativar alto contraste' (id contraste, aria-pressed) in the blue top bar, kept across pages in localStorage, whose body.darkroom styles put links in #ffff00 and other text in #fff on #000. G174 (a control that switches to a presentation with sufficient contrast) is a sufficient technique for 1.4.3 in Understanding 1.4.3, and the toggle seems to meet its test (visible near the top, white icon on dark blue, the alternate view meets 4.5:1 for this text). Auditors reasonably disagree on whether that makes the default text pass, so the label is uncertain even though the default presentation fails.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Main-menu link 'exposições' (11.5px, bold, not large text). The site's own stylesheet, which loaded in the capture and is the same live, sets '.menu li a{color:#999999}'; the capture measured #999999 on #f6f6f6, 2.64:1, so claimTrue is yes and the text fails 4.5:1 in the presentation users get once they close the popup (the overlay was hidden for the measure, which matches that view). Nothing in the live page differs. Skeptic check: the page has a native 'Ativar alto contraste' button (#contraste) whose body.darkroom styles turn this text white or yellow on black, so G174 was considered; it does not hold up, because G174 requires the alternate version to conform to every Level A/AA criterion, and the darkroom version keeps this page's other failures (the popup's img close control with no role, name or keyboard access; the newsletter e-mail field with no autocomplete). True positive.

patch.before: CLIQUE AQUI
patch.after: Agendamento Geral

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale:
First of three 'CLIQUE AQUI' links in the hero text block, to /agendamento-geral ('Agendamento Geral'). The block is one div whose lines are split by
; the snapshot's readingText reads '... AGENDAMENTO DE GRUPOS CLIQUE AQUI ...', so the text 'AGENDAMENTO DE GRUPOS' comes right before this link in the same sentence and block, with no punctuation between. That is programmatically determined link context (G53), and it tells the purpose (book a group visit). The first half of the claim holds (three same-text links, three destinations), but 'nothing around this one tells it apart' does not (claimTrue no). The element passes 2.4.4; only 2.4.9 (AAA) would fail. Live HTML is identical (captureDiffers no). False positive: the ancestor text in the evidence lists the three labels and then the three link texts at the end, which hides which label goes with which link, so the checker lacked the ordering it needed (context_missing).

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale:
The first of three 'CLIQUE AQUI' links in the hero's opening-hours block, leading to /agendamento-geral (page 'Agendamento Geral'). The three links are direct children of one div, each on its own line (separated by

) right after its lead-in, and the snapshot's readingText for that div reads '... AGENDAMENTO DE GRUPOS CLIQUE AQUI ...'; the live HTML is identical. So the text in the same sentence/paragraph as the link, immediately before it, states its purpose (G53), which tells the three apart; the claim's 'nothing around this one tells it apart' is false. Identical link texts in the links list are a 2.4.9 (AAA) matter, not 2.4.4. The packet's ancestor text strips the links and appends them after all three lead-ins, which hides the pairing from a reader of that context, hence context_missing.

ref: #popupe > div > img
subject: img click
message: This element listens to click, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as img, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The close button of the popup that covers the home page on load: with no role, no alt, no tabindex. It works as a button but is exposed as an image with no name, so assistive technology does not announce a control (F59 pattern), and it cannot be reached by keyboard either (2.1.1). The claim states exactly this (claimTrue yes). The live page serves the same popup and markup (captureDiffers no). Fails 4.1.2; true positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'X' close image of the Polo Catavento popup (#popupe), '', with no role, no alt, no tabindex; fecharpop() hides the popup, so it is a user interface control. The live page serves the same popup and markup. It is exposed as an image with no control role and no name, so it fails 4.1.2 for the reason the claim gives (it also fails 2.1.1 and 1.1.1). No technique or alternative makes this element itself expose a role.

ref: #govsp-rodape > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > a
message: The link text "SIC" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.rationale: Footer link 'SIC' to sic.sp.gov.br, in the São Paulo government footer next to 'Ouvidoria' and 'Transparência' (separate divs, no heading, no title), so it has no programmatic context. 'SIC' is the standard name (Serviço de Informações ao Cidadão) of the access-to-information service that Brazilian public sites must link to, and the link text names that destination; I lean pass, which makes 'does not tell where the link goes' not quite true (claimTrue no), and treat an unexpanded abbreviation as a 3.1.4 (AAA) matter. But an acronym with no expansion or context is a point where auditors reasonably disagree on 2.4.4, so the label is uncertain. Live link is the same; the missing footer stylesheet in the capture does not touch the text (captureDiffers no).

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Government footer link 'SIC' to sic.sp.gov.br, in its own div next to 'Ouvidoria' and 'Transparência', with no title, aria-describedby, preceding heading or same-paragraph text (true of the capture and of the live page). Skeptic reading: the link text is the name of the service it leads to (Serviço de Informações ao Cidadão, the standard label of Brazilian access-to-information services), so it does say where the link goes; an unexpanded abbreviation is a 3.1.4 (AAA) matter, stricter than 2.4.4. But competent auditors could reasonably hold that the bare acronym does not convey purpose to many users, so the label is uncertain.

ref: #edit-termo
subject: Buscar
message: The text "Buscar" has at most 2.85:1 contrast with what is behind it (#999999 on #ffffff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input title="Buscar" data-drupal-selector="edit-termo" class="form-text form-control" type="text" id="edit-termo" name="termo" value="" size="60" placeholder="Do que você precisa hoje?">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field #edit-termo: empty value, title 'Buscar' (its accessible name, which is never shown) and placeholder 'Do que você precisa hoje?'. claimTrue: no visible text 'Buscar' exists in or near the field. The snapshot's pixel measurement for 'text' (883 pixels, #999999 on #ffffff, 2.849:1, axe reason pseudoContent) matches the placeholder measurement exactly. So Rampa measured the placeholder and labelled it with the accessible name, which makes the sentence false as worded. elementFails: the only visible text in the field is the placeholder. Bootstrap's .form-control::placeholder rule sets it to #999 on the field's white background, 14px italic at weight 400, which is 2.85:1, below 4.5:1. No 1.4.3 exception applies, and the placeholder is the field's only visible cue because there is no visible label. The screenshot crop shows light grey italic text on white. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same input, and the live CSS still sets #999 for the placeholder and #fff for the field, so nothing differs. Read in good faith, the claim points at this field's real defect (its text at #999 on #fff, 2.85:1, 14px) and only gets the string wrong, so it is a true positive. It repeats the placeholder finding on the same element.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the search field #edit-termo. Its value is empty, its title is "Buscar" and its placeholder is "Do que você precisa hoje?". No text "Buscar" is shown on screen: it is only the title attribute, which supplies the accessible name. The snapshot's pixel measurement for this input (883 #999999 pixels, axe reason pseudoContent) is the placeholder's glyphs. My crop of the screenshot over the field shows only #999999 text on #ffffff, 2.85:1. So the sentence about a text "Buscar" is false of the capture. The input does fail 1.4.3 through its placeholder. Bootstrap 3 sets .form-control::placeholder to color:#999 on a white field, with no override in the live CSS. The site's Contraste switch (G174) does not rescue it: its contrast-mode rule targets '.header-search input', but this form is .celepar-busca, so the field stays white with #999 placeholder text. The live page matches the capture. The colours, size and element are the real defect's, but the claim names a text that does not exist. The placeholder-contrast finding on the same input reports this defect correctly. Competent auditors could reasonably disagree on whether a claim about a text "Buscar" names the placeholder failure, so the label is uncertain.

ref: #bloco-governo-digital > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > h2
subject: heading click
message: This element ("Serviços para você!") takes keyboard focus and listens to click, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as heading, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale:
The element is

Serviços para você!

at the top of the 'Serviços para você!' services block. claimTrue: the snapshot shows it focusable (tabindex 0), with a click listener recorded through CDP, and exposed as heading level 2 with no control role, as the sentence says. elementFails: the site's script binds a click on this h2 that toggles the class show-mobile on its container. In the theme CSS that class only matters under @media (max-width:575px), where the h2 gets cursor:pointer and a caret icon, the Dança/Música/Teatro buttons and service lists are hidden (display:none), and clicking the h2 shows them. So on phones, and on desktop browsers zoomed until the viewport is 575 CSS px or narrower, the h2 is the expand/collapse control for the block. It is still exposed as a heading, with no button role and no aria-expanded state. That is the F59 pattern under 4.1.2 (role and state not exposed). It also has no keyboard handler, a further 2.1.1 problem. At the 1280 px viewport Rampa captured, the click changes nothing visible, but the element is the same on the page users receive at narrow widths. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same markup, the same script and the same CSS, and the desktop capture matches the desktop page, so no capture difference touches the claim. The claim names this failure: a scripted, focusable control exposed only as a heading.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale:
The element is

Serviços para você!

, the title of the services bar. In the snapshot it is focusable, has a click listener, and is exposed as a level-2 heading with no control role, so the factual parts of the claim hold. Looking for a reason it could be wrong, I read the site script: the only click handler is jQuery's on '#bloco-governo-digital .header-bloco-governo-digital h2', and it toggles the class show-mobile on the header. In the live CSS that class only does something inside @media (max-width:575px). There the Dança/Música/Teatro buttons and service lists stay hidden until the h2 is clicked, and the h2 gets cursor:pointer and a caret icon. So at the captured 1280px width the click does nothing and the heading is not a control. But on phones, and at high zoom (the Reflow case), the same page uses the h2 as a disclosure button. A screen reader announces it only as a heading, with no button role and no expanded/collapsed state, which is the F59 kind of 4.1.2 failure. It also fails 2.1.1, because Enter on a focused h2 does not fire click. The claim names this failure: it works as a control but is exposed as a heading, so it is not announced as a button. The live HTML and scripts match the capture (same h2 with tabindex=0, same handler). The viewport difference is part of the page users receive, not a capture artefact. A desktop-only reading would pass it, but the narrow layout is part of the same page at the same address, so no reason against the finding holds up.

ref: #cookie-category-propaganda
message: The label "Propaganda" does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Propaganda' checkbox in the cookie preferences alertdialog 'Aviso de Cookies'. Its <label for> reads 'Propaganda' and sits in a list of categories (Necessários, Estatísticos, Propaganda). Directly below it is the description 'Cookies de propaganda são usados para rastrear preferências dos visitantes...'. claimTrue: a checkbox takes no entry. In its captured context the label names the cookie category the checkbox turns on, which is what the control is for, so the sentence's premise that the label leaves the user without knowing what to enter does not hold. elementFails: 2.4.6 asks labels to describe topic or purpose, and Understanding 2.4.6 says they may be short when the context makes them clear. Inside a dialog headed 'Aviso de Cookies', next to the other cookie categories and with its own description, 'Propaganda' clearly means advertising cookies, so the label meets 2.4.6. captureDiffers: the live HTML ships the same eu_cookie_compliance popup, with the same checkbox, label and description, shown to visitors who have not chosen yet, as in the screenshot, so nothing differs. Rampa demanded that a checkbox label 'say what to enter', a different rule from what 2.4.6 requires, so the finding is a false positive.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the "Propaganda" checkbox in the cookie consent dialog, under the heading "Aviso de Cookies". It is labelled by <label for="cookie-category-propaganda">Propaganda</label>, next to the categories "Necessários" and "Estatísticos". The description right under it reads "Cookies de propaganda são usados para rastrear preferências dos visitantes ... vídeos institucionais exibidos através do YouTube." A checkbox takes no input, so the claim's premise that the label should say what to enter does not apply. For a checkbox the label has to say what the choice is, and "Propaganda" does: it names the cookie category being allowed. That is why I answer no to claimTrue. 2.4.6 asks only that labels describe topic or purpose, and Understanding 2.4.6 does not require long labels or labels that carry instructions. In this cookie-category list the one-word category name describes the purpose. The live page's eu_cookie_compliance settings hold the same label, label/for association and description, and an ordinary first-time visitor gets the dialog, so the capture does not differ. Asking a checkbox label to say "what to enter" applies a text-field instruction standard (closer to 3.3.2) that 2.4.6 does not require.

ref: #homeSearch
message: The label "Suggested:" does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the home page search field (input type=search, role searchbox), labelled by a visible <label for=homeSearch>. In the capture the label reads "Suggested:" and the field holds an auto-typed suggestion ("State Parks" in the tree, "Jobs near me" in the screenshot), so the sentence is true of the capture: "Suggested:" names the shown suggestion, not what to enter. On the live page the source label is "Search"; the page script (scripts.min.js, home.typer) sets it to "Suggested:" on load while it types rotating suggestions, and on focus it sets the label to "Search:" and clears the field, restoring "Suggested:" on blur when the field is empty. So the capture matches what users get at rest; the focus-time label is page behaviour, not a capture difference. My lean is that the element meets 2.4.6: whenever someone moves into the field to type, its label is "Search:", and at rest the searchbox role, the adjacent Search button and the visible suggestion make the purpose clear. But at rest, and for screen reader users reading in browse mode, the label of a text field is "Suggested:", which does not describe its purpose, and competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether that resting label fails 2.4.6, so the label is uncertain. The auto-typing suggestion animation that loops without a pause control is a separate concern under 2.2.2.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the home-page search field (input type=search, id homeSearch). Its label element reads "Suggested:" in the capture, which gives the accessible name "Suggested:". That label does not say what to enter, so claimTrue is yes. The skeptic's reason against the finding is the page's own script. The static HTML label is "Search". The live scripts.min.js 'typer' sets it to "Suggested:" only while it types example queries into the field at rest ("State Parks" and "Jobs near me" in the capture). On focus it runs halt(), which sets the label to "Search:" and clears the value. So any user who goes into the field to type, by keyboard, mouse or a screen reader moving focus there, gets the label "Search:", which does describe its purpose. At rest, "Suggested:" sits next to an example query and a magnifier button named "Search". Read that way, the element passes 2.4.6, and I answer elementFails no. captureDiffers is no: the live HTML, script and search.json give the same resting state that the snapshot and screenshot show, and the focus-time label is a state change, not a capture defect. Still, a screen reader user in browse mode who does not focus the field hears only "Suggested:" as its name, and whether the name change on focus is announced depends on timing. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether the resting label fails 2.4.6, so the label is uncertain.

ref: #categoryAll
subject: All categories / Category
message: The visible label "All categories" is not in the field's accessible name, "Category", which comes from aria-labelledby: people using speech input say what they see, and the field does not answer to it.
html: <input type="radio" name="level_1_types" id="categoryAll" value="0" checked="" aria-labelledby="category">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the radio #categoryAll in the Category fieldset. Its visible label, a <label for> beside it, reads "All categories" (seen in the screenshot), but the input also carries aria-labelledby="category", which points at the legend and overrides the native label in the accessible name computation, so its name is "Category" (the snapshot records nameFrom aria-labelledby). "All categories" is not contained in "Category", so the claim is true of the capture, and the element fails 2.5.3 by documented failure F96 (accessible name does not contain the visible label text): a speech-input user saying the label they see will not activate it. The live page (fetched 2026-11-21) has the same markup for this fieldset as the snapshot, with no script that rewrites aria-labelledby, and the screenshot is fully styled and matches it, so captureDiffers is no. The claim names exactly this failure, so true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'All categories' radio (#categoryAll) has a visible <label for="categoryAll">All categories</label> next to it (screenshot), but aria-labelledby="category" overrides that label, and the CDP accessible name is 'Category'. 'All categories' is not contained in 'Category'. This is failure F96 of 2.5.3: a speech user saying 'click All categories' gets no match, and 'Category' matches all five radios. I looked for a reason it passes and found none. No exception applies, the label is the radio's own visible text label, and the live HTML has the same aria-labelledby on the radio, so the capture does not differ. The claim names exactly this failure.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the testimonial carousel's indicator list, an ol with role=tablist holding ten li elements with role=tab. In the snapshot no li has aria-selected, and the accessibility tree reports selected=false for all ten, including the one with class 'active', so the claim holds of the capture. The live HTML is the same, and the page's Bootstrap 3.4.1 carousel script only moves the 'active' class between indicators and never sets aria-selected. On the page users receive, a screen reader therefore cannot tell which tab, meaning which slide, is current, though users can change it by clicking. A state the user can set is not programmatically determinable, so this fails 4.1.2. The tabs also have no accessible names, which is a second 4.1.2 problem. The claim names the missing selected state, which is a real failure. I found no difference between the capture and the live page.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the testimonial carousel's ol.carousel-indicators (role=tablist) with 10 li role=tab dots, which Bootstrap 3.4.1 makes clickable through data-slide-to. In the snapshot the first li has class "active" and is drawn as the filled dot, but all ten tabs are exposed with selected=false and none has aria-selected, so the claim holds for the capture. Duplicating the headline is a redundancy that axe and most audit practice treat as best practice; whether a thumbnail alt that names the story instead of describing the photo fails 1.1.1 is a point on which competent auditors split (some fail it as not describing the image, or as a non-null alt on an image that should be decorative, F39; others pass it because the alt identifies the story the image illustrates). The crop shows a police custody photo of a man (the article captions him Apollo Simms, the driver) beside a photo of a woman drinking through a straw (Natasha Denman, the girlfriend). The alt is the headline, describing a fatal 84mph crash into roadworks that the image does not show, so the claim holds of the capture, though the alt does name the two people pictured. auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header link 'Cymraeg', the Welsh name of the Welsh language, on a page with html lang="en". It has no lang attribute in the snapshot's rendered DOM or in the live HTML, so it inherits English and a screen reader reads the word with English pronunciation. The claim is true of the capture. Understanding 3.1.2 gives this exact case among its examples: links to other language versions show the language's name in that language, with a lang attribute on each link (e.g. lang="de" on 'Deutsch'). It is not a proper name of the kind the exception means, nor vernacular English. It fails 3.1.2, for the reason the claim names. The live HTML fetched on 2026-11-21 has the same markup and alt text as the snapshot, and the screenshot is a fully styled page, so no difference touches this claim.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header link 'Cymraeg' (Welsh for 'Welsh') in a page with html lang='en'; neither the link nor any ancestor has lang='cy', in the snapshot or in the live HTML (the only lang='cy' strings there are CSS selectors). claimTrue yes. Skeptic checks: the proper-name and single-word exceptions do not save it, because Understanding 3.1.2 says single words count as the surrounding language unless a change is clearly intended, and in a language switcher it is: Example 2 of that document is this very case, language links marked with lang. An English voice would mispronounce the word, so the human language of this phrase is not programmatically determined. The element fails 3.1.2 for the reason the rule states. The live page fetched on 2026-11-21 has the same markup for this element, and the screenshot is fully styled and matches it, so no capture difference touches this.

subject: What’s On
message: The text "What’s On" has at most 2.41:1 contrast with what is behind it (#000000 on #4a4a4a…#4b4b4b), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a gradient). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: 'What's On' is the first link of the fixed header's primary nav, black 14px/900 text. Over dark content the header's blur is tinted at most 30% white (live gate.css/script.js), and in the screenshot the pixels behind the link are about #4d4d4d (the claim reads #4a4a4a-#4b4b4b, 2.41:1, near the blurred left edge; either way about 2.4-2.5:1). That is far under 4.5:1, so the text fails 1.4.3 whenever the black Explore More cards or the black footer band are under the header. The capture matches the live behaviour.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'What’s On' link in the fixed header's primary nav. In the capture's screenshot the bar is drawn over the black 'Explore more' cards, and sampling the pixels of this word (x 30-140, y 7080-7098) gives #000000 type on #4a4a4a-#4d4d4d (lighter near the card's left edge), about 2.41:1, so the claim holds of the capture. The live gate.css (versioned 13 Nov, before the capture) gives .site-header no background, only a backdrop-filter blur, and the live script.js tints that blur with rgba(255,255,255,0.3) at full strength when the black header type sits on a ground with no contrast; over black that is #4d4d4d, the exact colour Rampa measured. Users reach that state whenever they scroll the fixed bar over the black 'Explore more' cards or the black footer (at the foot of the page with an 800px window the bar sits over the footer). Skeptic checks: at the snapshot's own scroll position (bar at y=5844) the bar was over white and black-on-white passes, but that is another scroll state of the same page, not a capture artefact, and WCAG gives no exception for text that is legible only at some scroll positions; the bar has no solid background in any state on desktop (only while the phone menu is open); the type is 14px weight 900, below the 18.66px bold large-text size, so 4.5:1 is the right threshold and 2.4:1 even misses 3:1. No reason to dismiss it holds up: the element fails 1.4.3 in a state users get, and the claim names that failure.

subject: Comunicação
message: The text "Comunicação" has at most 2.13:1 contrast with what is behind it (#a3afbf on #fafafa), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the text of the breadcrumb link "Comunicação" (14px, weight 500, not large text). The live theme CSS sets .breadcrumb li .breadcrumb-link {color:#a3afbf} on #content {background-color:#fafafa}, which is 2.13:1, below the 4.5:1 1.4.3 requires. In the screenshot the area is under the cookie dialog's 50% black backdrop; undone, the darkest glyph pixel is about #a2aebe on #fafafa, about 2.16:1, which confirms the claim's values. The backdrop is probably why axe-core could not decide, but it does not change the colours measured. The live page fetched today has the same breadcrumb markup and CSS, so the capture does not differ in any way that matters.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the text of the breadcrumb link "Comunicação" (the link to /comunicacao), 14px at weight 500. The snapshot records #a3afbf from CSS on a measured #fafafa, 2.131:1, with axeReason bgOverlap: the fixed cookie modal covered it, which fits the claim's 'an element over or under it'. The screenshot's pixels under the 50% backdrop (#7d7d7d background, text down to #51575f) undim to #fafafa and about #a3afbf, and my own calculation gives 2.13:1 (claimTrue yes). The live theme main.css has '.breadcrumb li .breadcrumb-link{color:#a3afbf;font-weight:500}', with the same colour on hover, on the #fafafa page background. That is normal-size text in a working link, not a logo, inactive or incidental, so it needs 4.5:1 and fails 1.4.3 (elementFails yes). Reasons I tested for the finding being wrong: the modal backdrop only dims the page until it is closed, and Rampa measured the undimmed colours. The Rybená widget's optional contrast modes are not a verified conforming alternate (G174) and leave the default presentation failing. The live CSS matches the capture (captureDiffers no).

subject: Buscar
message: The placeholder "Buscar" has a contrast of 2.26:1 with the field (#757575 on #702826). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field. Its placeholder "Buscar" is the only visible text label the field has besides a magnifier icon. The live theme CSS gives .busca-param a transparent background and color #afb7c7 but no ::placeholder rule, so Chrome's default placeholder colour (#757575) is used over the dark red header (#702826). The screenshot agrees: it is dimmed by the cookie dialog's 50% black backdrop, and once that is undone the header measures #702826 and the darkest placeholder pixel about #747070, which is about 2.1-2.3:1 for 14px normal-weight text. Firefox's default (inherited colour at reduced opacity) would also give about 2.5:1. Placeholder text that is shown conveys information and is text under 1.4.3, so the claim names the real failure. The live HTML and CSS fetched today match the capture, and the backdrop does not change the measured colours.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search field, whose placeholder "Buscar" is its only visible text label (beside a magnifier icon). The snapshot records the placeholder colour #757575 from CSS and a measured background of #702826, 2.256:1, at 14px weight 400. I checked the screenshot: it was taken under the cookie modal's 50% black backdrop, and the field's pixels are #381413 with text pixels up to about #3a3838, which undimmed come to about #702826 and #757575. I also worked out the ratio myself and got 2.26:1 (claimTrue yes). The live theme CSS gives .busca-param a transparent background over the dark red header, typed text colour #afb7c7, and no ::placeholder rule, so the browser's default placeholder colour applies (#757575 in the captured Chrome). Placeholder text is text, here it labels the field, and it is not inactive, decorative or incidental, so it needs 4.5:1 and fails 1.4.3 (elementFails yes). Reasons I tested for the finding being wrong: (1) The 'aria-hidden' state comes from the open cookie modal hiding the content behind it and does not change what is drawn. (2) The Rybená widget's contrast modes, listed on the site's /acessibilidade page, could be read as G174. That does not hold up: it is a third-party overlay, nothing shows its output gives this text 4.5:1 (an inverted mode would keep the ratio low), and the default presentation is what fails. It is the only content of a link to /unidades-organizacionais/comissao-de-etica (UFU's Ethics Commission). claimTrue is yes: the link holds only this image, and the alt names a topic, not the Ethics Commission page itself. elementFails is no: because the image is the link's only content, 1.1.1 asks for a text alternative that serves the same purpose (G94/H30). The alt repeats the banner's text, which is all a sighted user gets too, and it signals the ethics topic the destination covers. That gives screen-reader users the same information about where the link leads. Asking the alt to name the exact destination page is stricter than 1.1.1 requires, so the cause is criterion_misapplied. captureDiffers is no: the live HTML has the same img, alt and href, and the screenshot shows the banner as in the crop.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the first image of the three-tile campaign grid, the only content of a link to /unidades-organizacionais/comissao-de-etica (page title 'Comissão de Ética'). As worded the claim is literally true of the capture: the image is the link's only content (title is empty) and its alt names a theme rather than the destination page. But the image is an image of text reading '#QUESTÃO de ÉTICA' with decorative figures, and the alt 'Questão de ética' reproduces that text, which is exactly the cue sighted users get for the link; it also names the topic of the destination (ethics, leading to the ethics committee). The text alternative therefore serves the equivalent purpose that 1.1.1 asks for, and nothing in 1.1.1, H30 or F30 requires the alternative to be more specific about the destination than the visible image is. Requiring the alt to name the target page is a stricter rule than the criterion. The live HTML has the same link, image and alt, so the capture does not differ.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Acesso à informação' link in the federal gov.br bar at the top of the page (rendered in upper case), going to gov.br/acessoainformacao. claimTrue is yes: the capture also has 'Acesso à informação' in the collapsed main menu and an 'Acesso à Informação' button in the footer, and both go to UFU's own /acesso-a-informacao. So the text is shared by links to two different places (three links counting the footer button, so the count of 2 is slightly off). Its list item holds only the link, its nav has no label, it has no title and no heading comes before it, so nothing programmatic sets it apart. elementFails, in my reading, is no: the text does state the purpose (the access-to-information section required by Brazil's LAI) and the link delivers that, at the federal level. Understanding 2.4.4 presents different link text for different destinations as advice, not as a requirement of the criterion (tools map that check to 2.4.9). But a user who meets both links in a links list cannot tell the federal portal from UFU's own page, and competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether that leaves the purpose undetermined, so the label is uncertain. captureDiffers is no: the bar is injected by barras.ufu.br/barra_2.0.js, and the script I fetched builds the same markup (nav#menu-barra-brasil, same href, no label or title), while the live HTML has the same menu and footer links.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Acesso à informação' link of the federal gov.br bar (injected by barras.ufu.br/barra_2.0.js, present in both the snapshot and the live page), leading to www.gov.br/acessoainformacao. The claim holds of the capture: UFU's own visible 'Acesso à Informação' button (and a hidden menu item) lead to /acesso-a-informacao, and this link's list item, the unnamed nav, the preceding 'GovBR' link and the absence of any earlier heading or title give no counted context to tell them apart. Against a failure: the link text itself describes the destination's purpose (the access-to-information portal), and WCAG 2.1 does not require different texts for different destinations; Understanding 2.4.4 only says it 'helps' for links with different purposes to have different text, and the identical-links check is usually mapped to 2.4.9. My own reading is that the element passes, but whether 'federal portal versus UFU's own LAI page' is part of the purpose 2.4.4 requires the text to convey is a point competent auditors would reasonably disagree on, so the label is uncertain. The bar script served now has the same link, so the capture does not differ.

subject: Sou Estudante
message: The text "Sou Estudante" has at most 4.15:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #9d7628), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.rationale: The element is the label text of the header button 'Sou Estudante' (white uppercase bold text on a gold pill). In the screenshot the button area is solid #9d7628 with #ffffff text; I compute 4.15:1 for that pair, below 4.5:1, and the text (10.9px bold, 14px at most in the theme CSS) is far from large-text size, so the claim holds of the capture. The live theme CSS still sets the nav button to background-color #9D7628 with color #fff and the markup is unchanged, so users receive the same pair and the text fails 1.4.3 for exactly the reason the claim gives.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the text of the header menu button 'Sou Estudante'. The live theme main.css sets this nav-link to background-color #9D7628 with color #fff, and the screenshot's button pixels are #9d7628 with white glyphs; white on #9d7628 computes to 4.15:1. The text is about 10.9px bold (0.775rem on this layout), far below the 18.66px bold large-text threshold, so 4.5:1 applies. I looked for a reason it could pass (a background image, an overlay, large text, a logotype exemption) and found none; the overlapping icon is what made axe abstain, not something that changes the colours. The capture matches the live CSS. The claim names the real failure.

ref: #_com_liferay_dynamic_data_mapping_form_web_portlet_DDMFormPortlet_INSTANCE_formFooter_ddm\$\$Email\$WQ1E6EK5\$0\$\$pt_BR
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input aria-describedby="_com_liferay_dynamic_data_mapping_form_web_portlet_DDMFormPortlet_INSTANCE_formFooter_ddm$$Email$WQ1E6EK5$0$$pt_BR_fieldFeedback" aria-required="true" dir="ltr" id="_com_liferay_dynamic_data_mapping_form_web_portlet_DDMFormPortlet_INSTANCE_formFooter_ddm$$Email$WQ1E6EK5$0$$pt_BR" lang="pt-BR" name="_com_liferay_dynamic_data_mapping_form_web_portlet_DDMFormPortlet_INSTANCE_formFooter_ddm$$Email$WQ1E6EK5$0$$pt_BR" placeholder="Digite seu Email" class="form-control ddm-field-text" type="text" value="">

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the newsletter e-mail field in the footer. Its label element ('E-mail', associated with for=) is hidden on the live page by the theme rule 'footer#footer .content-newsletter ... form label { display: none }', so the only visible cue is the placeholder 'Digite seu Email'. The captured Chromium accessibility tree gives the textbox an empty name (labelledby points to the hidden label, which contributes nothing), so the claim is true of the capture. Whether this fails 4.1.2 is open: by HTML-AAM the placeholder is a name source once the label yields nothing, axe-style checks would pass the field, and NVDA/JAWS normally announce the placeholder, yet Chrome itself exposes no name. I could not run a browser to confirm Chrome's computation independently, and competent auditors would disagree, so uncertain. The hidden label with a placeholder-only visible label is in any case a clearer 3.3.2 / 1.3.1 problem. The live form config (same label, placeholder, showLabel) and CSS match the capture.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the newsletter e-mail input in the footer. The snapshot's Chrome accessibility node has name '' with a labelledby relation to a label 'E-mail' that is display:none; the live theme CSS confirms it (footer .content-newsletter form label {display:none}), and the screenshot shows no visible label, only the placeholder 'Digite seu Email'. So the claim that the browser computes no name holds in the capture. The skeptic's reasons against a clear failure: HTML-AAM lists the placeholder attribute as a name source after label and title, axe accepts a non-empty placeholder as a name, other engines may fall back to it, and Chrome still exposes the placeholder to assistive technology, which NVDA and JAWS commonly speak, so 'announces only textbox' is not shown. Whether a placeholder-only name meets 4.1.2 is a point competent auditors split on, and the capture matches the live page, so the label is uncertain.

subject: e-mail
message: The text alternative "e-mail" repeats the image's file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the envelope icon (e-mail.svg, alt and title 'e-mail') in the fifth link of the top share bar under the article header, 'Compartilhar' followed by facebook/twitter/linkedin/whatsapp/e-mail. The crop shows a small envelope. claimTrue: yes. The alt repeats the file name stem 'e-mail' and is what a screen reader reads for the image. elementFails: no. For an envelope icon in a share group, 'e-mail' is an adequate text alternative: it conveys the image's meaning and the option's function, sharing by e-mail. A file name that is itself a correct description does not fail 1.1.1 (F30 concerns names that are not alternatives). The wrapping <a> has no href and is exposed as generic, a possible 4.1.2/2.1.1 issue outside this criterion. captureDiffers: no. The live server HTML has the same share component with loading placeholders (class 'e-mailloading') that hydrate into these icons, consistent with the snapshot. The bar is sticky ('fixed-compartilhar'), so it is blank at its static position in the stitched screenshot, but the same bar appears with its icons elsewhere in the screenshot. My fetch cannot run scripts, but nothing indicates users receive a different alt. Label: false positive, because the rule equates matching the file name with failure instead of judging equivalent purpose.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the envelope icon (e-mail.svg, as the crop shows) in the top share bar, after "Compartilhar" and the Facebook, X, LinkedIn and WhatsApp icons: the share-by-e-mail control. claimTrue: yes; alt="e-mail" equals the file name and is what a screen reader reads. elementFails: no; the file name is meaningful and "e-mail" correctly names what the envelope means in a share bar, so the alt is a real alternative and F30 (file names that are not alternatives) does not apply. The wrapping <a> lacks an href and is exposed as generic, a 4.1.2/2.1.1 issue rather than 1.1.1. captureDiffers: no; the share bar is script-rendered, so the server HTML cannot show it, but the snapshot is a scripted render consistent with the screenshot and the server-rendered header icons follow the same alt pattern. The rule treats any alt that matches the file name as placeholder text, a stricter test than WCAG's.

Its alt is only the credit " (Imagem: Magnific)"; the title and a visible, unassociated caption below say 'Liberdade de convicção política também deve ser respeitada nas relações de trabalho.' claimTrue: no. The alt is a source credit and describes no visual content, so it does not 'describe something the image does not show'; the problem is omission, not mismatch. elementFails: yes. A credit is not a text alternative (F30): the name says nothing about the work card or the handover, which carry the employment theme, including the card's printed text. Even if the image were treated as illustrative and covered by the caption, the non-null credit alt keeps it from being ignored (F39's test). The title attribute is only a description and not a sufficient technique for the alternative. captureDiffers: no. The live server HTML has the identical img alt/title and img-info caption, and the screenshot shows the styled image and caption at the snapshot's position. Label: the claim's wording is imperfect but, read in good faith, it points at the alt failing to describe the image, which is the real failure. True positive.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the article's second-section illustration, an 878x498 collage of a hand holding a phone showing a WhatsApp group with a blurred list next to a shop front crossed by a red prohibition sign, i.e. boycott lists aimed at shops. Its alt is only the credit line " (Imagem: Arte Migalhas)"; the title attribute (exposed only as a description) and a visible caption div below, not associated as a figcaption, say 'Listas de boicote por motivação política podem gerar responsabilização por abusos.' claimTrue: no. The alt does not describe anything that is missing from the image. It is a credit and describes no visual content at all, so the sentence's 'describes something the image does not show' is not literally what happens. elementFails: yes. The accessible name is a photo credit, which is not a text alternative (F30). If the image is informative, the name does not convey what it shows. If it is treated as illustrative and covered by the caption, it should be ignorable (alt=""), but a non-null credit is announced instead (F39's test). The title is not a sufficient technique for the short alternative, and the credit is already in the visible caption. captureDiffers: no. The live server HTML (fetched 2026-11-21) has the same img alt/title and the same img-info caption, and the screenshot shows the styled page with the image and caption where the snapshot puts them. Label: read in good faith, the claim says the alt does not match the image, which points at the real defect: the alt leaves out everything the image conveys. That makes it a true positive. The adjacent caption is a mitigating factor, but a credit-only alt is still a standard 1.1.1 failure.

ref: #menu-item-93 > div:nth-of-type(1) > button
subject: Institucional Submenu
message: The icon of this button ("Institucional Submenu") has at most 2.63:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#90a1b9 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: A submenu toggle in the main navigation: a separate <button> (aria-label "Institucional Submenu") whose only visible content is a small chevron SVG drawn in currentcolor. claimTrue: the snapshot records the stroke colour from CSS as #90a1b9 on #ffffff, and my own pixel sample of the screenshot at the icon gives #90a1b9 as the darkest pixel on white, 2.63:1. elementFails: the chevron is the only visual sign of this control and of its drop-down function; the text beside it belongs to a separate link (href="#"). Understanding 1.4.11 says such a down-arrow "is required to understand that there is drop-down functionality", so it needs 3:1 (G207), and 2.63:1 falls short. captureDiffers: the screenshot is fully styled, and the live html i fetched on 2026-11-21 has the same markup for this element, so nothing differs. The claim names this failure, so true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the submenu toggle button "Institucional Submenu" in the main navigation: a <button> whose only content is a 10px chevron SVG drawn with stroke=currentcolor. claimTrue: the live global-custom-css sets ".bricks-nav-menu li button { color: #90A1B9 }", the header is white, and #90a1b9 on #ffffff is 2.63:1, as stated; the button shows nothing but the icon (the label text is a separate link). elementFails: I looked for a reason the chevron would be exempt: it is not decorative and not duplicated by text, since the adjacent text "Institucional" is a separate href="#" link and does not say there is a submenu; Understanding 1.4.11 says a menu arrow must meet 3:1 and that the arrow is what shows the drop-down functionality. The colour comes from CSS, so this is not an antialiasing artefact. 2.63:1 is below 3:1. captureDiffers: the live CSS and markup are the same and the screenshot shows the styled header. The claim names the real failure, so true_positive.

ref: #brxe-anqolv
subject: Diretoria e Comissões
message: The link text "Diretoria e Comissões" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

patch.ref: #brxe-anqolv
patch.before: <a id="brxe-anqolv" class="brxe-text-link" href="https://sbpt.org.br/portal/diretoria-em-exercicio/" rel="Diretoria e Comissões" aria-label="Diretoria e Comissões">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: A footer link whose visible text is "Diretoria e Conselho", but aria-label="Diretoria e Comissões" sets its name. It leads to /diretoria-em-exercicio/. The next link ("Comissões e Departamentos", to a different page) has the same aria-label. claimTrue: two links share the name and lead to different places, and the only context is the h2 "Institucional", so the sentence holds. elementFails: screen-reader users cannot tell this link from the other, and its name also promises committees the board page does not cover, so its purpose cannot be determined. It also fails 2.5.3. captureDiffers: The live HTML I fetched on 2026-11-21 has the same markup for this element. true_positive.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the footer link with visible text "Diretoria e Conselho" and aria-label "Diretoria e Comissões", to /diretoria-em-exercicio/ (the board page). The link to /comissoes-e-departamentos/ has the same aria-label. claimTrue: the accessible name is shared by two links with different destinations, and the preceding heading "Institucional" does not tell them apart. elementFails: screen reader users hear "Diretoria e Comissões" for both, which overstates this link's target and does not distinguish it; my lean is yes. But the name does start with "Diretoria", which matches the board page; Understanding 2.4.4 treats distinct text for different destinations as advisable rather than required; the rubric counts the accurate visible text; and the clearer failure is 2.5.3 Label in Name. captureDiffers: the live markup is the same.
