message: The link text "Foto de coral no fundo do mar" does not match where the link goes.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: An image-only link in the Pesquisa e Inovação image group, name from the alt 'Foto de coral no fundo do mar', to a Revista Universidade article 'Pesquisadores da Ufes embarcam em expedição científica para mapear fundo marinho na Zona de Fratura de Romanche' (checked live). claimTrue: the link text describes a photo, not the article it opens. In DOM order the heading just before is 'Assistência estudantil', which does not help, and the link has no title or aria-describedby of its own, so by the rubric's list its purpose cannot be determined and I lean to a failure. But the img inside the link has title equal to the article's headline (in the snapshot it is the image's accessible description, and a tooltip on hover), so the purpose is programmatically present within the link itself; whether a title on the link's only child counts as the link's context is not settled by H33 or the rubric, and competent auditors would split on it, so uncertain. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same alt, title and href; the screenshot shows the image still blurred by lazy loading, which does not touch the claim.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is an image-only link named by its alt, 'Foto de coral no fundo do mar'. It leads to a Revista Universidade article about a Ufes expedition mapping the seafloor in the Romanche Fracture Zone. It has no aria-label, title or aria-describedby, and it sits in no paragraph, list item or cell. The heading before it in document order is 'Assistência estudantil', from the previous section, because the 'Pesquisa e Inovação' h2 comes after the images. The claim is true of the capture: the name describes the photo, not the article, and the topics overlap only in 'fundo do mar'. I lean that it fails, since sighted users at least get the placement in the 'Pesquisa e Inovação' block, which AT users do not get programmatically. Against that, the photo has no caption, so sighted users could not tell it opens that article either. The 'ambiguous to users in general' exception is arguable, and the alt does point at the article's seafloor subject. The live page has the same alt and href. The screenshot shows the image blurred by lazy loading, which does not affect the name. Uncertain.

ref: #views-bootstrap-ingresse-na-ufes-block-1 > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > span > h5 > a
message: The link text "Pós-graduação" is shared by 5 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The link 'Pós-graduação' is one of four cards (Graduação, Extensão, Ensino a distância, Pós-graduação) in the 'Estude na Ufes' section and leads to PRPPG's 'Mestrados e doutorados da UFES' (checked live). claimTrue: the snapshot does have five visible links named Pós-graduação/Pós-Graduação going to two URLs (this one and a footer link to the PRPPG list; three Editais category labels to /categoria-edital/pos-graduacao), but 'nothing around this one tells it apart' is not so: it sits under the section heading 'Estude na Ufes', whose paragraph speaks of its master's and doctoral courses. elementFails: the link text alone gives the purpose, postgraduate study at Ufes, and the destination is that list of programmes; 2.4.4 does not require link texts to be unique, and the Editais labels are category tags in another section. It passes. Cause: a uniqueness rule stricter than the criterion. captureDiffers: live HTML is the same.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the card link 'Pós-graduação' (inside an h5) in the 'Estude na Ufes' block, leading to prppg.ufes.br 'Mestrados e doutorados da UFES'. The claim is true of the capture. Five non-hidden links are named Pós-graduação or Pós-Graduação: this one and the footer link go to prppg, and three Editais category tags go to /categoria-edital/pos-graduacao. Under the round's context rule only its own h5 precedes it. But 2.4.4 asks whether each link's purpose can be determined. It does not ask that links with the same text be told apart; that is the ACT rule for 2.4.9 (AAA), and Understanding 2.4.4 only says it 'helps'. On a university home page, 'Pós-graduação' states this link's purpose, and the destination matches it. The live HTML is the same. This is a stricter rule than the criterion.

ref: #swiper-wrapper-57854b09c955fd1f > div:nth-of-type(4) > a > div
subject: Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26
message: The text alternative "Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26" is the name a camera or a screenshot tool gave the file: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.
html: <div class="elementor-carousel-image rocket-lazyload" role="img" aria-label="Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the div role="img" on the active slide ("1 / 7") of the "Depoimentos" video carousel. Its aria-label is "Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26", the default name the macOS screenshot tool gives a file in Portuguese. In the browser's accessibility tree that string is the image's name and also the name of its link: the screen-only "Reproduzir" span sits inside the role=img and is dropped. So a screen reader announces the file name, and the claim is true. The background image (data-bg, lazy-loaded) is a still from the video: a man speaking in an ESPM library, with subtitles. The other slides are named after the person ("giovanna tecno"), but this name says nothing about the image. That is failure F30, so 1.1.1 fails. The live HTML has the same aria-label and data-bg. The capture did not paint the lazy background (the crop shows only the play icon), but that touches the crop, not the claim about the alternative.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: A div with role=img and aria-label "Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26", the macOS Portuguese default screenshot name, is the thumbnail of a testimonial video slide; because role=img hides the screen-only "Reproduzir" span, the browser also gives the link that name (ax name in the snapshot). The capture lacked the lazy-loaded background image (the crop shows only a play icon on dark red), but the label is identical live. I downloaded the image: it is a still of a man speaking, with ESPM branding and subtitles. The label conveys none of that, and even if the slide were treated as decorative a file name is not an acceptable alternative (F30, F39). The claim names the failure.

ref: #swiper-wrapper-57854b09c955fd1f > div:nth-of-type(11) > a > div
subject: Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26
message: The text alternative "Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26" is the name a camera or a screenshot tool gave the file: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.
html: <div class="elementor-carousel-image rocket-lazyload" role="img" aria-label="Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the same image as finding 46a53f7f31a3, on the Swiper loop clone of that slide (class swiper-slide-duplicate, also labelled "1 / 7"). The clone has no aria-hidden or inert, and its link is focusable, so screen reader and keyboard users meet it. Its aria-label is the screenshot file name "Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26", which the browser exposes as the image's name and the link's name, so the claim is true. The image is a still of a man speaking in an ESPM library, and the file name conveys none of it: failure F30, so 1.1.1 fails. Swiper builds the clones in any browser that runs the page's scripts, and the source markup matches the live HTML. The unpainted lazy background in the capture does not touch the claim.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the Swiper loop duplicate of the same slide (swiper-slide-duplicate, off to the right of the viewport). It has the same role=img div with aria-label "Captura de Tela 2025-10-28 às 11.39.26", a screenshot tool's file name. The snapshot shows the duplicate is not hidden from assistive technology: its link is exposed with that name, so screen reader users meet it too. The live HTML has the same label. The real image is a speaker still from the video, which the label does not convey (F30). The claim names the failure.

ref: html > body > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > b > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > img
subject: tecnologos-personagem-geral
message: The text alternative "tecnologos-personagem-geral" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: html > body > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > b > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > img
patch.to: Mulher jovem e criança em um ambiente criativo e acadêmico com elementos gráficos coloridos.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This hero img has alt and title "tecnologos-personagem-geral", a file-name slug. The image is a collage of three young women on a yellow parallelogram with patterned shapes: a schoolgirl with a backpack, a woman in a mustard blazer and a graduate in cap and gown. Together they suggest the path from student to graduate. Taken literally the sentence is false: the slug ("general character") does not name anything the image lacks. It is a file name that conveys nothing of what the image shows. The element fails 1.1.1 (F30). If one treats the image as decorative it should have alt="", and the slug is announced anyway. Read in good faith as the rubric fixes it, saying the alternative "describes something the image does not show" points at an alternative that leaves out what the image conveys, so the claim names the failure. The live HTML is the same.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The large hero image is a collage of three women: a schoolgirl with a backpack, a professional in a yellow blazer, and a graduate in cap and gown. Its alt and title are the file slug "tecnologos-personagem-geral", in the snapshot and live. Taken literally the claim is off: the slug names nothing the image lacks, since it does show characters. But the alt leaves out everything the image conveys, which is the case the rubric gives as an imperfectly worded claim that names the defect. If the image were judged decorative, a file-name alt would still fail (it should be empty). The element fails 1.1.1 under either reading.

ref: html > body > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > b > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > img

Some might call the stamp decorative because the scholarship is described further down. Even then it should have alt="", and the file name would still be announced, so it fails 1.1.1 either way. The live HTML has the same alt and title.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The hero seal image shows a stamp reading "100% ESPM" ringed by "BOLSA SOCIAL". This promotes the full social scholarship, and no nearby hero text says so, so the image is informative. Its alt and title are "selo-bolsa-social-1.png", the file name with its extension, in the snapshot and in the live HTML. The words in the file name hint at a seal, but the alt leaves out the 100% and is a file name, which F30 documents as a failure. I found no technique that makes it pass. The claim names the failure.

ref: #gallery-1 > figure:nth-of-type(4) > div > a > img
subject: logo ceb
message: The text alternative "logo ceb" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: #gallery-1 > figure:nth-of-type(4) > div > a > img

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: This img with alt "logo ceb" is the only content of a link in the "Apoio:" gallery. The link's href is the full-size logo file and it opens an Elementor lightbox with that same logo. The figcaption "logo ceb" is display-hidden and only referenced by aria-describedby. "All its link holds" is true, but the alt names a logo, which is what the link opens, so "does not say where the link leads" only half holds. The element does fail 1.1.1, mainly for another reason: the logo spells out "Clube Empreendedor Brasil" (crop and screenshot), and the acronym "ceb" appears nowhere in it, so the alternative does not give the organisation's name. It also leaves out that the link enlarges the logo. Auditors would reasonably disagree about whether the claim names this failure. Many accept a plain image description on a link to a larger copy of the same image, and the claim's point, the link's destination, is not the acronym problem. The live markup is the same (alt, lazy-load attributes, hidden caption, lightbox link). The packet's link name shows noscript HTML, but the browser's accessible name is "logo ceb", so this does not touch the claim.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the Clube Empreendedor Brasil logo in the "Apoio:" gallery, alt "logo ceb", as the only rendered content of a link (the noscript copy is not rendered; the ax name is "logo ceb"). The link's href is the same logo PNG, and it opens in an Elementor lightbox. So the alt does say what the link leads to, the CEB logo, and the claim's reason does not hold. The alt may still fail 1.1.1 for another reason: the initialism "ceb" appears nowhere in the image and does not convey the organisation name the logo spells out. The claim does not name that reason. The live HTML matches the capture.

ref: html > body > b > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > p:nth-of-type(1)

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the first footer paragraph. Its span holds ESPM's tagline "The Marketing Powerhouse" (CSS shows it in capitals), followed by a zero-width space. The p, the span and their ancestors have no lang attribute. The only lang on the page is html lang="pt-BR", both in the snapshot and in the live HTML I fetched on 2026-11-21, so a screen reader speaks the English phrase with Portuguese pronunciation. The claim is true of the capture. The phrase is an English slogan, not a proper name, a technical term or a phrase that has become part of Brazilian Portuguese, so no 3.1.2 exception applies and the element fails. The live markup is the same as the capture.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The footer paragraph holds a span reading "The Marketing Powerhouse" on a page whose html lang is pt-BR. Neither the span, the p nor any ancestor has a lang attribute, in the snapshot and in the live HTML I fetched, so the capture matches the page. I looked for an exception: the phrase is ESPM's English tagline, not a proper name, technical term or a phrase that has entered the Portuguese vernacular (only "marketing" has), so a pt-BR voice would mispronounce "The" and "Powerhouse". The claim names exactly that failure of 3.1.2.

ref: html > body > div > div > div > div > div > b > div:nth-of-type(8) > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > h3
message: The heading "Bolsas Sociais Meritocráticas de" says nothing about the content under it.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The h3 "Bolsas Sociais Meritocráticas de" heads the scholarship card. Under it come the counters "100% (Integral e gratuita) ou 50% (Parcial)", a paragraph on the two kinds of scholarship (full 100% and partial 50%) and a "Como pedir a bolsa" button. The heading ends in a dangling "de" that leads into the percentages, but it names the card's topic, merit-based social scholarships. So the claim that it says nothing about the content is false, and the heading meets 2.4.6. In the capture the counters still read 0% because the count-up animation had not run (the live markup has data-to-value 100 and 50). That does not change whether the heading describes its content, and the paragraph states 100% and 50% in both versions. The checker had the following text in the element's context and judged wrongly.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The h3 "Bolsas Sociais Meritocráticas de" heads a card whose content is the two scholarship values (Integral e gratuita 100%, Parcial 50%) and a paragraph explaining the two types of scholarship. The trailing "de" is awkward because the sentence goes on into the counters, but the heading still names its topic: social merit scholarships. So the claim that it says nothing about the content under it is false. The capture shows the counters at 0% because their animation had not run (live they count up to 100 and 50), but the heading and the paragraph are the same, so that difference does not change this judgment.

ref: html > body > div > div > div > div > div > b > div:nth-of-type(8) > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > h3
message: The heading "ou" says nothing about the content under it.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This h3's whole text is "ou" ("or"). It sits between the counters "100% (Integral e gratuita)" and "50% (Parcial)" and is exposed as a level-3 heading, so a screen reader's heading list offers "ou". That word describes no topic or purpose, and it does not describe "(Parcial) 50%", the content that follows it. The W3C ACT rule "Heading is descriptive", mapped to 2.4.6, applies to any element with the heading role and fails here. The claim is true and names this failure. The same element also fails 1.3.1, because text that is not a heading is marked up as one. The capture's 0% counters (live values 100 and 50) do not matter here, and the live markup is the same.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: "ou" (or) is the conjunction between the two scholarship counters, marked up as an h3 by the page builder. It is the same in the live HTML. As exposed to assistive technology, it is a level 3 heading that describes no topic, so the claim is true and a literal reading of 2.4.6 fails it. The concrete counter-reason: the text is not a heading in the content at all, and misusing heading markup is classically logged under 1.3.1 (F43), not as a non-descriptive heading under 2.4.6. Competent auditors would reasonably split on which criterion this belongs to, so the label is uncertain.

ref: #barra > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > div > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
message: The link text "Professor" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The link is "Professor" (its teacher icon is aria-hidden) in the header's two-item list "Estudante | Professor". It goes to portal.espm.br; its sibling "Estudante" goes to portaldoaluno.espm.br, the student portal. Under the rubric, the link's context is only its own text: its list item holds nothing else, no heading comes before it, and it has no title or aria-describedby. So the sentence is true: the text does not name a destination and nothing counted adds to it. But 2.4.4 asks for the link's purpose, not its address. On a university site, "Professor" in the utility bar is the usual entry to the faculty area, and the word itself gives that purpose. A sighted user gets nothing more than the same word and icon. The link meets 2.4.4: the claim demands that the text say where the link goes, which is stricter than the criterion. The live link is the same. My fetch of the destination got a Vercel checkpoint (429), so I could not check it beyond its domain. In the full-page screenshot the fixed header was painted mid-page and is missing from the top, but that does not change the link text.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: "Professor" is the second link of the top utility bar ("Estudante" goes to portaldoaluno.espm.br, "Professor" to portal.espm.br), with an aria-hidden teacher icon. It has no title, describedby or preceding heading, and its list item holds only that word, so the link text alone has to carry its purpose. In a university header, a link named after its audience tells you its purpose: the area for professors. Sighted users also get only the word "Professor" and an icon that repeats it, so if anything were unclear it would be unclear to users in general, which 2.4.4 exempts. Demanding that the text name the exact destination is stricter than the criterion. The live HTML matches the capture.

ref: #acritica-search-toggle
subject: Buscar / Abrir busca
message: The visible label "Buscar" is not in the field's accessible name, "Abrir busca", which comes from aria-label: people using speech input say what they see, and the field does not answer to it.

patch.ref: #acritica-search-toggle
patch.before: <input class="peer/search sr-only" id="acritica-search-toggle" type="checkbox" aria-label="Abrir busca">
patch.after: <input class="peer/search sr-only" id="acritica-search-toggle" type="checkbox">

html: <input class="peer/search sr-only" id="acritica-search-toggle" type="checkbox" aria-label="Abrir busca">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header's search toggle: a visually hidden (sr-only) checkbox with aria-label="Abrir busca", operated through <label for="acritica-search-toggle"> whose visible content at desktop width is the text "Buscar" plus an aria-hidden magnifier icon (the screenshot shows "Buscar" with the icon at the top right of the blue header). claimTrue: the snapshot shows exactly this, the aria-label overrides the label so the accessible name is "Abrir busca" (nameFrom aria-label), and "Buscar" does not occur in it; calling a checkbox a "field" is loose wording, not a false statement. elementFails: the component's visible label is "Buscar" and its accessible name "Abrir busca" does not contain that text ("busca" is a different word from "Buscar", and a speech user saying "click Buscar" targets a name that does not hold it), which is failure F96 of 2.5.3. captureDiffers: the live HTML fetched now has the same label, the same checkbox and the same aria-label, and no script changes them (the toggle works by CSS peer-checked); the screenshot is fully styled. The claim names this failure, so the label is true_positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the visually hidden (sr-only) checkbox that opens the header search form. Its visible label is <label for="acritica-search-toggle"> holding the text "Buscar" (shown at md widths and up) and an aria-hidden magnifier icon. The aria-label "Abrir busca" overrides that label, so the accessible name is "Abrir busca". claimTrue: the snapshot shows exactly this (the label is LabelText with an empty name of its own, and the checkbox's name comes from aria-label). Calling a checkbox a "field" is loose wording, but what the sentence says holds. elementFails: the screenshot at 1280 px shows "Buscar" next to the icon. "Buscar" is not a substring of "Abrir busca": "busca" is a different word form (noun, not the verb), and 2.5.3 and failure F96 ask for the visible label text itself to be in the name. A speech user saying "clicar Buscar" targets a control whose name lacks that word. I looked for a reason it passes and found none: the label is the programmatically associated, visible label of this control; the label element has no role or name that speech software could target in its place; only at narrow widths is the label icon-only, and there "Abrir busca" would be fine, but desktop users get the text. captureDiffers: the live HTML fetched now has the same label, the same span and the same aria-label, and the screenshot is a fully styled page. Label: true_positive, since the claim names the actual 2.5.3 failure.

ref: html > body > main > section:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > a > h1
message: The heading "Praia da Ponta Negra é interditada para banho em Manaus" names a different topic than the content under it.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the h1 of the homepage's lead story, inside the story link, "Praia da Ponta Negra é interditada para banho em Manaus". claimTrue: the content it heads in the snapshot and screenshot is the dek "Interdição foi anunciada após o rio Negro atingir 15,94 metros; medida segue recomendação do Serviço Geológico do Brasil" and the byline, which are about the same topic; what follows are three separate story links (Maria do Carmo, a car overturning, tranças afro) in a related-stories list without headings, which do not make the heading name a different topic than its own content, so the sentence does not hold. elementFails: the heading describes the story it introduces, and the destination page carries the same headline, so it meets 2.4.6; the unheaded list after it (and the use of an h1 for a teaser on a homepage) is at most a structure question, not a non-descriptive heading. captureDiffers: the live page has the same lead story, headline and dek (only the relative time moved from 5 to 6 hours). The model had the dek in the link's text and judged wrongly, so the label is false_positive with cause model_error.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the h1 of the homepage's lead story card, inside the link to that article. The content right under it, in the same link, is the summary "Interdição foi anunciada após o rio Negro atingir 15,94 metros; medida segue recomendação do Serviço Geológico do Brasil" and the byline: the same topic as the heading. The destination page's title and heading match too. claimTrue: the content under the heading is about the beach closure, so the sentence does not hold. What follows the card is three unheaded links to other stories and then the "Agora" aside with its own h3s, and the page's later sections all have their own h2s. elementFails: 2.4.6 asks that a heading describe the topic or purpose of its content, and this heading describes its story accurately. That the following links have no heading of their own, or that the page's single h1 is a story headline rather than a page title, is a heading-structure matter (1.3.1 or best practice), not a 2.4.6 failure, and 2.4.6 does not require headings. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same h1, summary and following links (only the relative time differs, "há 6 horas"), and the screenshot is styled. Label: false_positive. The model had the context and misjudged the heading against content that is not its section: model_error.

ref: html > body > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > form > button
subject: Buscar
message: The icon of this button ("Buscar") has at most 2.63:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#b99c63 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the icon-only submit button (aria-label 'Buscar') of the header search form; its only visible content is an SVG magnifier with fill: currentColor. The live page's inline CSS gives the button color #b99c63, a transparent background and a 1px #b99c63 border, on the white header, which matches the capture and the screenshot crop (a thin gold magnifier in a gold circle). #b99c63 on #ffffff computes to 2.63:1, below the 3:1 that 1.4.11 asks for graphics required to identify a component; the magnifier is what identifies this button, and the circle border has the same colour. Only the hover/focus state (white on #1d4a7d) has enough contrast. The claim states exactly this failure: true positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the search submit button in the header. Its only visible content is an SVG magnifier (aria-hidden; the name 'Buscar' comes from aria-label and is not visible). In the live page's inline CSS the button has a transparent background, color #b99c63 with fill: currentColor, and a 1px #b99c63 circular border, all on the white header. Sampling the screenshot's pixels gives #ffffff behind the icon and #b99c63 for the strokes: 2.63:1, below the 3:1 that 1.4.11 asks for the visual information that identifies a component (G207). I looked for a reason it might pass. White on #1d4a7d applies only on hover and focus, not in the default state. The border is the same low-contrast gold. The button is not inactive, and its styling is the author's, not the browser default. Neither the neighbouring search field nor the fact that Enter also submits exempts the button's own icon. The claim names this failure, and the live CSS matches the capture.

ref: #conjur-content > p:nth-of-type(4) > a
message: The link text "deslocamento coletivo" does not match where the link leads: a page titled "Buser é proibida de operar linha por extrapolar autorização".

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: Inline link 'deslocamento coletivo' in the sentence 'Nesse desenho, os estados conservam competência para disciplinar o deslocamento coletivo entre municípios de seus territórios', under the h2 'Competência estadual'. It leads to a related ConJur story about Buser being barred from operating an intermunicipal line beyond its authorisation. The claim reads mismatch from the difference between the anchor words and the destination title, but the link's sentence (its programmatically determined context) is about regulating collective transport between municipalities, and the destination is precisely a ruling on intermunicipal collective transport, so the purpose (more on intercity collective transport regulation) can be determined; 2.4.4 does not require the text to repeat the destination title. Some auditors are stricter with keyword links in news text, but the topical match here is direct. Live HTML identical. False positive: it applied a 'text must match the title' rule.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is an inline link, 'deslocamento coletivo', in the sentence 'os estados conservam competência para disciplinar o deslocamento coletivo entre municípios de seus territórios'. It leads to a ConJur article about Buser being barred from running an intermunicipal line. The claim is literally true: the link text differs from the destination's title. But 2.4.4 does not ask link text to match the destination's title. The sentence and paragraph that frame the link are its programmatically determined context, and the destination is related coverage of that topic (state regulation of intermunicipal collective transport). Whatever more a reader cannot tell before following the link, a sighted reader cannot tell either. That is the criterion's 'ambiguous to users in general' exception, illustrated in WCAG by the 'guava' example: all readers are unsure, so the person with a disability is at no disadvantage. The live HTML is the same.

ref: html > body > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > form > input
message: The label "Pesquisar..." does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The header search text field (name 'q') in a form with role='search', next to the 'Buscar' button; it has no label element, and its only visible and computed label is the placeholder 'Pesquisar...' (dark #1a1a1a text, visible in the screenshot). 2.4.6 asks that labels describe topic or purpose; 'Pesquisar' (Search) in a search form says the field takes a search query, which is what to enter, so the claim does not hold and the label is descriptive. A placeholder-only label may raise 3.3.2 or 1.3.1 questions (it disappears on typing), but that is another criterion and not what the claim says. Live HTML identical. False positive: it asked more of the label than 2.4.6 does.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the header search field, inside a form with role='search' next to a 'Buscar' button. Its only label is the visible placeholder 'Pesquisar...'. 2.4.6 asks that a label, where there is one, describe the topic or purpose of the field. 'Pesquisar...' does: it says the field is for searching the site, which tells users to type search terms. So the claim that it 'does not say what to enter' does not hold, and asking for more is a stricter rule than the criterion's. Relying on a placeholder with no programmatic label may raise questions under 1.3.1, 3.3.2 or 4.1.2, but it is not a 2.4.6 failure. The live HTML and CSS show the same input and placeholder.

ref: #conjur-content > p:nth-of-type(6) > a

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: Inline link 'atendimento dos passageiros' in 'a proteção à iniciativa privada e à competição admite condicionamentos destinados à segurança e ao atendimento dos passageiros', under the h2 'Competência estadual'. skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is an inline link, 'atendimento dos passageiros', in the sentence 'a proteção à iniciativa privada e à competição admite condicionamentos destinados à segurança e ao atendimento dos passageiros'. It leads to a ConJur article on TRF-1 upholding the closed-circuit requirement for Buser. The claim is literally true: the text does not match the destination's title. But 2.4.4 does not require that match. All the context a sighted reader has, the sentence and paragraph about restrictions on transport companies, is the link's programmatically determined context. Whatever is left unclear about where the link goes is equally unclear to every reader. ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > article:nth-of-type(2) > a > div > figure > img

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > article:nth-of-type(1) > a > div > figure > img

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > article:nth-of-type(5) > a > div > figure > img

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > article:nth-of-type(4) > a

subject: generic click
message: This element ("FRETE GRÁTIS EXCLUSIVO NO APP") takes keyboard focus and listens to click, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as generic, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.
evidence: role generic · click · "FRETE GRÁTIS EXCLUSIVO NO APP"

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the promotional top bar "FRETE GRÁTIS EXCLUSIVO NO APP", a div.promotionalTopBar__container. claimTrue: yes. The snapshot shows it as role generic, focusable, with a click listener and no role attribute. elementFails: yes. In the live HTML it has tabindex="0" and cursor:pointer, and no role. The component's live script (cea.store-ds PromotionalTopBar) renders it as a div with onClick=handleBarClick and tabIndex set only when a redirectLink exists, which means it works as a link to a redirect target. Assistive technology gets no role for it (F59, 4.1.2: name, role, value). Separately, it has no key handler, so Enter likely does nothing, a probable 2.1.1 issue too. captureDiffers: no. The live markup matches the capture in every point that matters; only the bar's background colour differs, which does not touch this claim.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the promotional top bar div ("FRETE GRÁTIS EXCLUSIVO NO APP"). The snapshot's CDP tree gives it role generic, focusable and a click listener. Looking for a collector artefact, I checked the live HTML: the div has tabindex="0" and cursor:pointer, and has no role or name. The site's own bundle (cea.store-modules PromotionalTopBar) wires onBarClick to handleBarClick, which sets window.location.href to the configured redirectLink. The page config sets that to https://www.cea.com.br/baixe-app-cea, with an empty coupon. So the div really works as a link that takes focus, yet it exposes no control role: this is failure F59 of 4.1.2. claimTrue: the message states exactly this. captureDiffers: the live markup matches. The bar's colour differs between the screenshot and the live inline style, but that does not touch this claim.

skeptic.rationale: The element is the site logo inside the Cookiebot consent banner (img#CybotCookiebotDialogPoweredbyImage, a 46x46 data-URI PNG of the Cork City Council crest, in a div, not a link), with alt="logo". claimTrue: the captured alt is the bare word "logo", a generic placeholder that names the kind of image, not its content, so the sentence holds. elementFails: I looked for a way it passes and found none. If the crest is informative (it identifies whose banner this is), "logo" cannot replace it without losing the organisation's identity, which is F30 (placeholder text like "image" or "picture"). If it is decorative, a non-null alt is F39. Either way 1.1.1 fails. It is exposed to AT (ax role image, name from alt, not aria-hidden), and the snapshot gives it real bounds. Being third-party widget content does not exempt it. captureDiffers: the live Cookiebot configuration for this site's cbid sets logoAltText = 'logo', showLogo = true and a data-URI logo, and the banner is auto-hidden only below 600px width, so users at this width get the same alt. The full-page screenshot shows only the lower strip of the fixed banner (the Cookiebot wordmark row), not the crest, but that is a screenshot artefact of a fixed element, and the DOM, bounds and image crop agree with the live configuration. The claim names the real defect (placeholder alt), so true_positive.

The link has no aria-label or title, so the link's name is that string. claimTrue: the image is all the link holds, and the string neither names the destination nor reads as the council's name. elementFails: a functional image's alternative must convey its function, or at least the text in the image. A file-name-like string does neither (F30; H30/H37), so this fails 1.1.1. The link also gets no usable name, which is a related 2.4.4 problem. The claim's point, that the alternative does not say where the link leads, is the real defect of this functional image, read in good faith. captureDiffers: I fetched the live HTML, and the same <a class='global-header-logo' href='/en/'> holds the same img with the same alt. skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header logo image, the only content of the link a.global-header-logo (href="/en/"). Its name comes from contents, and the alt is a CMS media name that says neither home nor Cork City Council, so the sentence holds. elementFails: as a functional image, the alt must convey the link's purpose (Understanding 1.1.1 for controls, H30). At the least it should give the logo's text. A file-name-like token is the F30 failure (filenames and programming references). An auditor who accepts an organisation name alone for a home logo link would still fail this alt. captureDiffers: the live HTML fetched now has the identical anchor and img with alt="ccctransparentlogo-small". In the screenshot the cookie banner covers the header, but that does not change what the alt exposes. The claim says the alt fails to state the link's destination, which, read in good faith, names the functional-image failure, so true_positive.

patch.ref: #embeddedNavLinks > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > a
patch.before: Christmas Jumpers
patch.after: Women's Christmas Jumpers

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The link sits in #embeddedNavLinks, a nav landmark the header script fills client-side for every browser (seoClientSidePixelEnabled is true in the live config) and styles height:0; overflow:hidden; position:fixed: invisible on screen (the screenshot shows no such list) but not aria-hidden, so screen readers read it in browse mode and list its links even though they carry tabindex=-1. 2.4.4 therefore applies to it. It is "Christmas Jumpers" (women's knitwear filter) in the nested list under the CHRISTMAS item, which mixes women's, men's and general gift items in one flat list. claimTrue: the snapshot has the stated number of same-text links and destinations; no heading precedes the nav, the H81 parent item is only "CHRISTMAS", and the link has no title or aria-describedby. The preceding sibling item that says which department follows is not context under the rubric. elementFails: it, the men's one and a general "Christmas Jumpers" link share the text and the same parent, so its department cannot be determined. The claim names that failure. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same empty nav container with the same inline style and the same fill script; my fetch cannot run that script, but nothing suggests users get a different list.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: "Christmas Jumpers" link to women's Christmas jumpers. The link sits in #embeddedNavLinks, an SEO navigation the header script builds on the client for every visitor (seoClientSidePixelEnabled is true on the live page): a nav with inline style height:0; overflow:hidden; position:fixed, not aria-hidden, links with tabindex=-1. It is invisible and out of the tab order but in the accessibility tree (CDP role link), so screen reader users read it in browse mode and 2.4.4 applies. The builder drops the group labels that have no target (WOMENS OUTERWEAR, FOR HER, WOMEN'S OUTLET), so each top-level item holds one flat list. Its context under the rubric is its own list item and, by H81, the parent list item CHRISTMAS; no heading precedes it. CHRISTMAS mixes women's, men's and all-audience links in one flat list; the sibling items (Gifts for Her, Gifts for Him) that suggest the grouping are not context by the rubric. claimTrue: I recounted the links with this name in the snapshot (case-insensitive, including the visible teaser links) and the count and number of destinations match; inside CHRISTMAS the same text also leads to the men's and the all-audience Christmas Jumpers links, and nothing in the rubric's context tells this one apart. elementFails: a screen reader user hears identical link text in the same list for different departments and cannot tell which to follow; I looked for a skeptic's way out (aria-label, title, aria-describedby, a heading, H81 parent item, the hidden-SEO status) and none holds up. captureDiffers: the live page has the same empty nav that script fills, and the live /headerstatic/seo-content JSON it reads lists the same items and targets in the same order as the snapshot, so no difference touches this claim. The claim names that failure.
